deep.reconstruction:
This page is part of Gauss's mathematical diary (the 'Tagebuch', Cod. Ms. Gauss Math. 48 Cc). It covers entries of 30 Nov 1800 to Aug/Sept 1801, roughly Gray's nos. 113-121 (numbering from memory, may be off by one).

(1) Nov. 30 [1800], Braunschweig. Gauss records that he found the number of classes of binary quadratic forms by three methods.
- (i) An infinite product: in modern terms h is proportional to L(1,chi) = prod_p (1 - chi(p)/p)^(-1).
- (ii) An infinite sum: the Dirichlet series sum chi(n)/n.
- (iii) A finite sum of cotangents or of logarithms of sines.
Method (iii) is the closed evaluation of L(1,chi). For negative discriminants it gives h(-D) proportional to sum chi(n) cot(pi n/D) (equivalently a sum of n*chi(n)). For positive discriminants it gives h log(eps) = -sum chi(n) log sin(pi n/D).

(2) Dec. 3 [1800], Braunschweig. A fourth method, 'the simplest of all', for negative determinants. Let Ax+s, Ax+s', ... be the linear forms of the divisors of t^2 + D. The class number is then obtained purely from how many of the numbers s, s', ... there are. The diary states only that a count suffices. My reading (inferred, not on the page) is that the count is over a half-interval. In modern form: h(-D) = (1/(2 - chi(2))) * sum_{0<n<D/2} chi(n) for a prime D ≡ 3 mod 4, D > 3. That is, residues minus non-residues below D/2.

(3) Apr. 6 [1801], Braunschweig. Gauss notes that he has demonstrated the impossibility of reducing the division of the circle to equations of lower degree than his theory (Disq. Arith. sec. VII) prescribes. This is the necessity half of the constructibility criterion: an n-gon is constructible only if phi(n) is a power of 2, i.e. n = 2^k times distinct Fermat primes.

(4) Apr. 1 [1801]. A new method for determining the Jewish Passover. This was later published as 'Berechnung des jüdischen Osterfestes' (1802).

(5) Mid-May [1801], Braunschweig. A fifth proof of the fundamental theorem (quadratic reciprocity) by means of a theorem from cyclotomy. With P = the full circumference (2*pi) and n running over 0..a-1, the theorem reads:
- a ≡ 0 (mod 4): sum sin(2 pi n^2/a) = sqrt(a) and sum cos(2 pi n^2/a) = sqrt(a).
- a ≡ 1 (mod 4): sin-sum = 0 and cos-sum = sqrt(a).
- a ≡ 2 (mod 4): both sums are 0.
- a ≡ 3 (mod 4): sin-sum = sqrt(a) and cos-sum = 0.
Compactly, G(a) = sum_{n=0}^{a-1} exp(2 pi i n^2/a) = (1+i)(1 + i^(-a)) sqrt(a)/2, i.e. sqrt(a), 0, i*sqrt(a), (1+i)sqrt(a) for a ≡ 1, 2, 3, 0 mod 4. The magnitudes follow from |G|^2 = a when a is odd. The signs are exactly what Gauss could not prove until 30 Aug 1805 (next page). In 1801 the entry is therefore an assertion, presumably verified numerically. The proof was published in 'Summatio quarumdam serierum singularium' (1811).

(6) Sept. [1801]. A new, simplest and quickest method for finding the elements of the orbits of heavenly bodies. This is the Ceres orbit determination that led to Theoria motus (1809).

(7) Aug. [1801]. Gauss records that he has begun the theory of the Moon's motion.

No derivations are written out on the page; it is a log of results.
errors: No mathematical errors. The Gauss-sum table is correct for all four residue classes mod 4.

The signs (+sqrt(a)) in the table were not yet proved in May 1801. Gauss himself says on the next page that the proof took over four years (completed 30 Aug 1805), so at this date the entry is a conjecture, apart from the absolute values.

deep.surprise_reason: This is the famous mathematical diary, published by Klein (1903) and Werke X.1 and translated by Gray. All entries are well known. In particular, the anticipation of Dirichlet's class number formula and the Gauss-sum entries are standard historical facts.

The divisor form is written in the image as '□+D' (square + D), i.e. tt+D; the prime mark in the transcription is spurious.
